links.note: 1301 has the friend urge the woman to hold back her embrace and sulk (புல்லாது இராப் புலத்தை) so they can watch his pain 'a little' (சிறிது). 1302 states the limit that word implies: sulking is like salt in right measure, and letting it run on (நீள விடல்) is like salt in excess. Parimelazhagar reads the சிறிது of 1301 as already pointing to this rule.

1301 proposes not embracing (புல்லாது) in order to see his அல்லல்நோய். 1303 uses the same two words from the other side: leaving the one who sulks unembraced (புல்லா விடல்) is like giving அல்லல்நோய் to those already in distress (அலந்தாரை). Read together, the pain that 1301 treats as a brief test is the pain 1303 says must not be left standing.

In 1301 the friend wants the sulk kept up so that his suffering can be seen for a while. In 1329 the man himself wishes she would go on sulking (ஊடுக மன்னோ) and the night grow long so that he may keep pleading (யாம் இரப்ப). Both sides treat the sulk as something to prolong on purpose, hers to watch and his to beg.

1302 says sulking is like salt in fitting measure (உப்பு அமைந்தற்று) and too much of it is like salt in excess. 802 says a friend's liberties are a limb of friendship and that being salt to them (உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar glosses this as being sweet toward those liberties. In both, salt is what makes a close bond palatable, but only the love verse adds that the salt can be overdone.

1302 gives the measure: a little sulking seasons, a little too long spoils. 1306 gives the two failures by name: without துனி and புலவி, love is like கனி and கருக்காய், which Manakkudavar reads as overripe fruit and unripe fruit. Together they make sulking a matter of degree, judged by taste, in both verses through a food image.

1302 allows sulking in measure, like salt. In 1282 the woman says that when love comes filling to the size of a palmyra, one should not sulk even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). 1282 is a speech by a woman eager for union, so it limits 1302 for that moment and does not cancel it.

1303 says that leaving unembraced those who have sulked (புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்) is like giving sharp pain to those already suffering (அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்று). 1304 says that not appeasing those who sulk (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). The pair states one claim twice, once as added hurt and once as a finishing cut. Parimelazhagar takes both as the wife's taunt sending the man back to his other women.

1304 compares leaving a sulking lover unappeased to cutting an already withered creeper at its root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). 1030 says a family with no good man to prop it falls when trouble cuts it at the foot (இடுக்கண் கால் கொன்றிட வீழும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as an axe at the tree's base. Both picture a weakened plant that needed support and got the cut instead, once in love and once in the household.

1305 says that for men good in their qualities (நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு) the beauty (ஏர்) is the sulking in flower-eyed women; Parimelazhagar reads this as 'even for the faultless, sulking is sweet'. 1325 says the same in plainer terms: though without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft shoulders of the one they love has something in it (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). Manakkudavar reads 1305 differently, taking நல்லவர் as the other women.

1305, on Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man find beauty in her sulk even though he is good and blameless. 1321 gives her side: he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is what makes sulking possible. Both verses detach the sulk from any real offence.

1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like கனி and கருக்காய்; Manakkudavar takes these as fruit gone past ripeness and fruit not yet ripe. 100 says speaking unpleasant words when pleasant ones exist is like taking the unripe fruit while the ripe is there (கனி இருப்பக் காய் கவர்ந்தற்று). In 100 ripe is simply good and unripe bad; in 1306, on that reading, both ends are faulty and the right point lies between.

1306 puts it negatively: without quarrels, serious and light, love is fruit at the wrong stage. 1330 puts it positively: sulking is the pleasure of love (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்), and the pleasure of sulking is the embrace that follows. The chapter 133 verse states as a conclusion what 1306 argues by image.

1307 finds a pain inside sulking (ஊடலின் உண்டு ஆங்கு ஓர் துன்பம்): the thought of whether union will be delayed or not. In 1152 the woman says union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவு அஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). In both, a state counted as pleasant carries worry about what comes next.

1330 calls sulking the pleasure of love, provided the embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). 1307 fastens on that proviso: because one cannot be sure the union will not be long delayed (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்), the sulk has its own pain. 1307 is the reservation built into 1330's praise.

1308 asks what use it is to suffer where there is no lover who knows 'this one is hurt' (நொந்தார் என்று அஃது அறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 877, in the chapter on enemies, advises: do not voice your hurt to those who do not know you are hurt (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). The same roots நோ and அறி carry one rule in love and in statecraft: displayed pain is wasted on someone who does not perceive it.

1308 says the man's hurt is useless without a lover who recognises it. 1309 gives the general form: as water is sweet in shade, sulking is sweet only with those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). Parimelazhagar assigns both to the man, in a sulk that she is not answering.

In 1308 suffering is pointless when the other does not know or care that one suffers. In 1200 the woman tells her heart that reporting its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) is like trying to fill in the sea. Man and woman reach the same judgment from opposite sides of the couple.

1309 says water is sweet when it is in shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. 881 says even shade and water are bad if they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so are one's own people. Both use shade and water as the stock example of what is pleasant, and both make the pleasantness depend on a condition: love in the one, harmlessness in the other.

1309 limits the sweetness of sulking to those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே). 1323 asks whether any heaven matches sulking with those joined like water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both say the value of the sulk depends on the closeness of the two, and both use water to say it.

In 1310 the man, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's intent to join with one who leaves him to wither in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு) is just craving (அவா). In 1292 the woman scolds her heart for going to him even after seeing that he is not close to her (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்). Each blames the heart for running to someone who has shown no care.

1304 compares the unappeased sulker to a withered creeper (வாடிய வள்ளி) cut at the root. 1310 speaks of being left to dry up in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவார்). The wife's warning and the man's complaint use the same picture of a plant left without water; Parimelazhagar places 1310 in a sulk she does not answer.

1310 calls the heart's wish to join with one who neglects it mere craving. In 1255 the woman says the dignity of not going after those who have turned away (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the love-sick do not know. Both admit that desire overrides self-respect toward an indifferent partner.

In 1311 the woman refuses his chest (நண்ணேன் பரத்த நின் மார்பு) because all women feed on him with their eyes in common (பொது உண்பர்). 915 says the wise will not touch the mean charms of women whose charms are common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). She applies to a man the book's own reasoning about public women: what is பொது is not to be touched. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit by calling his chest their leavings.

In 1312 the woman says he sneezed while she was sulking, knowing (அறிந்து) she would have to say 'live long' and so speak to him. In 1253 the sneeze is the example of what happens without intention: desire comes out குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல். Parimelazhagar notes that 1312 treats a natural sneeze as a deliberate one, which is the subtlety the chapter title names.

In 1313 the man reports that even wearing a wreath makes her angry (காயும்): 'you wore it to show some woman'. In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet his way of showing tenderness can bring on a sulk. 1321 supplies from her mouth what the man's complaints in chapter 132 imply: the grounds are invented.

1311 gives her stated ground: every woman takes him in with her eyes (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). 1313 shows the same worry applied to a trifle: a wreath must have been put on to be shown to another woman (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர்). Her jealousy in both is about who sees him.

In 1314 he says 'we love more than anyone' (யாரினும் காதலம்) and she turns it on him: 'than whom, than whom?' (யாரினும் யாரினும்). 645 advises speaking a word only after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). The love scene shows that rule failing in a comic way: his own word, repeated back, is the one that beats him.

In 1314 'more than anyone' is heard as implying other loves; in 1315 'we will not part in this birth' (இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம்) fills her eyes with tears, because she hears a parting in the next. Parimelazhagar describes the move in 1315: she takes a plain statement as a hinting one. Both verses turn a strong assurance into an offence by what it leaves unsaid.

In 1315 a promise limited to this birth (இம்மை) makes her weep. 107 says the good remember through all seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்) the friendship of those who removed their distress. Her complaint measures his promise against the span the book itself uses for lasting bonds.

In 1316 he says 'I thought of you' (உள்ளினேன்) and she answers 'why did you forget?' (என் மறந்தீர்). In 1125 the man himself uses that logic: he would remember her qualities if he forgot them, but he does not know forgetting (உள்ளுவன் மன் யான் மறப்பின்; மறப்பறியேன்). Her inference in 1316 is the one he made in 1125, now used against him.

1316 has her treat remembering as proof of forgetting. In 1207 the woman, alone, says she does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்) and that even remembering burns. The standard she holds him to in 1316, never having forgotten at all, is the one she claims for herself in separation.

In 1203 the woman, apart from him, takes a sneeze that starts and dies away as a sign that he was about to think of her and did not (நினைப்பவர் போன்று நினையார்கொல்). In 1317 the same belief, that one sneezes when someone thinks of one, makes her weep: 'who thought of you, that you sneezed?' (யார் உள்ளித் தும்மினீர்). The sign she waited for in absence becomes evidence against him in his presence. Parimelazhagar cites this belief in his note on 1317.

In 1312 she suspects his sneeze was a trick to get the customary 'live long' out of her. In 1317 she gives that blessing (வழுத்தினாள்) and at once takes it back (அழித்து அழுதாள்) with a new suspicion. One sneeze is read two ways in the chapter, as a stratagem and as proof of another woman.

In 1317 sneezing brings the charge that some woman is thinking of him. In 1318 he holds the sneeze back (தும்முச் செறுப்ப) and she weeps anyway: 'are you hiding from me that your people think of you?' (நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ). The two verses close both exits: sneezing and not sneezing are both faults.

In 1253 the woman says she would hide her desire (மறைப்பேன்) but it comes out like a sneeze. In 1318 he does manage to hold a sneeze in, and the holding in is what she reads as hiding (மறைத்திரோ). Both verses pair the sneeze with concealment; in 1253 it stands for what cannot be hidden, and in 1318 hiding it is itself the offence.

In 1319 even his effort to appease her makes her angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்): 'you must be like this with others too'. 693 warns those who serve kings that once suspicion has arisen, clearing it is hard for anyone (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The court maxim and the bedroom scene describe the same trap: reassurance offered to a suspicious mind is taken as more evidence.

1304 says not appeasing one who sulks (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. In 1319 he does appease her (தன்னை உணர்த்தினும்) and that too is a fault. Taken together, the man is blamed in chapter 131 for not doing what chapter 132 shows cannot be done to her satisfaction.

1313, 1319 and 1320 share the frame '…even if I do X, she is angry (…இனும் காயும்), saying …'. In 1313 the act is wearing a wreath; in 1320 it is only sitting and looking at her (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும்), which she takes as comparing her with someone (யார் உள்ளி நோக்கினீர்). The series runs from adornment down to a silent look, so that no act of his is left free of suspicion.

In 1311 her objection is to other women's eyes on him (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). In 1320 it is to his eyes on her, which she thinks are really on another woman; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that she supposes he is matching her limbs against someone else's. The chapter opens and closes on the look as the place where she locates unfaithfulness.
